```plato
    // A dynamic solver body at a pose, with the given mass and principal moments.
    // The direct constructor for a caller that never authored a `RigidBody3D` — a
    // demo scene, or a test.
    DynamicBody(pose: Pose3D, mass: Mass, principalMoments: Vector3D): SolverBody3D
        => SolverBody3D(
            pose.Position,
            pose.Orientation,
            SpatialVelocity3D(Vector3D.Zero, Vector3D.Zero),
            mass.Amount > 0.0 ? 1.0 / mass.Amount : 0.0,
            InverseMoments(principalMoments),
            0.0, 0.0, 1.0);

    // An immovable solver body at a pose: no inverse mass, no inverse inertia, and
    // therefore no response to any impulse. The ground, and every wall.
    StaticBody(pose: Pose3D): SolverBody3D
        => SolverBody3D(
            pose.Position,
            pose.Orientation,
            SpatialVelocity3D(Vector3D.Zero, Vector3D.Zero),
            0.0,
            Vector3D.Zero,
            0.0, 0.0, 0.0);

    //==
    // # Forces, torques and impulses
    //
    // A force applied away from the centre of mass both accelerates and spins a
    // body; the pair of the two is a wrench (`SpatialForce3D`, declared in
    // `kinematics.types.plato`), and reducing an applied force to one is the whole
    // of what "applied at a point" means.

    // The wrench a force applied at a world point exerts about `centre`: the force
    // itself, and the torque r x F it makes about the lever arm.
    // (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torque)
    WrenchAbout(applied: AppliedForce3D, centre: Point3D): SpatialForce3D
        => SpatialForce3D(
            applied.Force,
            centre.Between(applied.ApplicationPoint).Cross(applied.Force));

    // The body after an authored impulse at its authored point.
    ApplyImpulse(self: SolverBody3D, applied: AppliedImpulse3D): SolverBody3D
        => ApplyImpulse(self, applied.Impulse, applied.ApplicationPoint);

    // The body after an explosion: an impulse directed away from the blast centre,
    // at full magnitude at the centre and falling linearly to nothing at the
    // radius, applied at the body's own centre so that it pushes without spinning.
    // A body outside the radius, or exactly at the centre, is untouched.
    ApplyImpulse(self: SolverBody3D, blast: RadialImpulse3D): SolverBody3D
    {
        var away = blast.Center.Between(self.Center);
        var distance = away.Magnitude;
        var falloff = (1.0 - distance / blast.Radius.Amount).Clamp(0.0, 1.0);
        return distance <= 0.0
            ? self
            : ApplyImpulse(self, away / distance * (blast.Magnitude.Amount * falloff), self.Center);
    }

    // The velocity decay factor of an exponential damping rate over a step:
    // exp(-rate * dt), which is the exact solution of dv/dt = -rate v and is
    // therefore stable at any step size, unlike the (1 - rate * dt) that a
    // first-order reading of the same rate would give and that goes negative once
    // the step is long enough.
    DampingFactor(rate: Number, seconds: Number): Number
        => (-rate * seconds).Exp;

    //==
    // # Integration
    //
    // SEMI-IMPLICIT (SYMPLECTIC) EULER, and the choice matters more than its two
    // lines suggest: velocity is advanced by the acceleration FIRST, and position
    // is then advanced by the NEW velocity.
    //
    //     v' = v + a dt          then          x' = x + v' dt
    //
    // Explicit Euler uses the OLD velocity for the position update. On the orbit
    // and the spring — the two motions a rigid-body engine spends its life
    // integrating — explicit Euler gains energy every step and the motion spirals
    // outward without bound, at any step size. Semi-implicit Euler is symplectic:
    // its energy error is bounded and oscillates rather than accumulating, so a
    // pendulum swings forever at very nearly the right amplitude instead of
    // winding up. It costs exactly the same arithmetic. There is no case for
    // explicit Euler in this library.
    //
    // Higher order was also rejected, for a different reason: velocity-Verlet and
    // RK4 both want to evaluate forces more than once per step, and a step that
    // contains a CONTACT SOLVE has no smooth force field to re-evaluate. The
    // accuracy those methods buy is spent on the smooth part of a simulation whose
    // error is dominated by the non-smooth part.
    //
    // Orientation is advanced by the quaternion rate q' = q + (omega (x) q) dt / 2
    // and renormalized. That is first order in the same sense, and the
    // renormalization is what keeps repeated products on the unit sphere.
    // (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-implicit_Euler_method)

    // The orientation after spinning at `angular` radians per second for
    // `seconds`, renormalized. The quaternion rate is half the angular velocity,
    // as a pure quaternion, multiplied onto the current orientation from the left.
    IntegrateOrientation(orientation: Quaternion, angular: Vector3D, seconds: Number): Quaternion
        => (orientation
            + Quaternion(angular.X, angular.Y, angular.Z, 0.0) * orientation * (0.5 * seconds))
            .Normalize;

    // The body with its velocity advanced by a wrench and gravity, then damped —
    // the FIRST half of a semi-implicit step. Gravity is an acceleration, so it is
    // added directly rather than through the inverse mass, and it is scaled by the
    // body's own multiplier; an immovable body has no inverse mass and so feels
    // neither the wrench nor, through the same zero, its own weight.
    //
    // The GYROSCOPIC term is omitted. Euler's equation has an extra
    // -I^-1 (omega x I omega) on the angular update, and it is what makes a
    // tumbling body with three different moments flip end over end. Integrated
    // EXPLICITLY, as it would have to be here, that term adds energy at every step
    // and a fast-spinning body diverges — which is why engines that want it solve
    // it implicitly, as its own small non-linear system. Omitting it is exact for
    // any body with two equal moments (every ball, cylinder and capsule here) and
    // costs a box its tumbling instability.
    IntegrateVelocity(self: SolverBody3D, wrench: SpatialForce3D, gravity: Vector3D,
        seconds: Number): SolverBody3D
    {
        var accelerating = self.InverseMass > 0.0;
        var linear = self.Velocity.Linear
            + (wrench.Force * self.InverseMass
                + (accelerating ? gravity * self.GravityScale : Vector3D.Zero)) * seconds;
        var angular = self.Velocity.Angular + AngularResponse(self, wrench.Torque * seconds);
        return WithVelocity(self, SpatialVelocity3D(
            linear * DampingFactor(self.LinearDamping, seconds),
            angular * DampingFactor(self.AngularDamping, seconds)));
    }

    // The body with its pose advanced by its current velocity — the SECOND half of
    // a semi-implicit step, which must run after the velocity is final.
    IntegratePose(self: SolverBody3D, seconds: Number): SolverBody3D
        => SolverBody3D(
            self.Center + self.Velocity.Linear * seconds,
            IntegrateOrientation(self.Orientation, self.Velocity.Angular, seconds),
            self.Velocity,
            self.InverseMass,
            self.InverseInertia,
            self.LinearDamping,
            self.AngularDamping,
            self.GravityScale);

    // The body with its pose advanced by its velocity PLUS a pseudo-velocity that
    // is not part of its motion: how the position pass's correction reaches the
    // pose without ever entering the body's real velocity.
    IntegratePoseWith(self: SolverBody3D, correction: SpatialVelocity3D, seconds: Number): SolverBody3D
        => SolverBody3D(
            self.Center + (self.Velocity.Linear + correction.Linear) * seconds,
            IntegrateOrientation(self.Orientation,
                self.Velocity.Angular + correction.Angular, seconds),
            self.Velocity,
            self.InverseMass,
            self.InverseInertia,
            self.LinearDamping,
            self.AngularDamping,
            self.GravityScale);
```
